content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper experiments a cross-domain self-supervised transfer learning approaches for predicting Alzheimer's disease endpoint based on brain MRI analysis.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

Significant implication for prognosis of Alzheimer's disease (AD). 

Weaknesses

1) "MRI" should be spelled out when first used. 

2) The authors show "Barlow Twins→ SimCLR" has the best performance but do not provide any intuition or mathematical support on why this is the case.  

3) The authors put together a "self-supervised learning platform" as described in Section 3.2. It's unclear which of the elements on this platform are part of this paper's contributions.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Lack of novelty in methodology or mathematical modeling.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this type of work is important for advancing prognosis of AD. But due to the lack of methodological or mathematical modeling innovations, this paper might be more appreciated in a different community.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The manuscript presents a learning strategy that pre-trains on both natural images and MRIs using self-supervised learning. The learned network is used to predict progression of Alzheimer's disease.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strength

Pooling 8k subjects from multiple studies on Alzheimer's disease

# Weakness

1. Taking 2D slices from 3D MRIs makes the method much less interesting and less impactful. Using 2D natural images to augment 3D MRI learning will likely have very limited clinical value.

2. Predicting Alzheimer's Disease outcome based on MRI data is probably one the most widely studied topics in the field of neuroimage computing. None of those prior works/results was mentioned here.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The manuscript is simple and written in a fairly clear fashion. The major issue is the lack of methodological contribution. Several existing self-supervised schemes were tested to augment 2D MRI slices with natural iamges. The results were not put together with the large body of existing research on Alzheimer's disease so the clinical impact is limited. Treating 3D MRIs as 2D slices are over-simplified and incompatible with the trend in 3D neuroimage computing.
content.summary_of_the_review: The manuscript does not meeting the criteria of ICLR due to the lack of novelty and comparison with SOTA results and methods.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Authors of this paper propose to use cross-domain self-supervised learning approach for disease prognostic modeling as a regression problem. Existing methods on various settings are investigated. Experiments show that self-supervised pre-training can be helpful.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

This is the first attempt to use self-supervised deep convolution neural networks on medical cross-domain datasets to predict CDRSB value of Alzheimer’s disease progression.

Four different experimental settings are studied, and conclusions are drawn.

Weaknesses:

Predicting the progression of Alzheimer’s disease solely based on CDRSB value is not well justified.

From modeling perspective, the discussions or comparisons of self-supervised deep convolution neural networks used in the experiments are missing.

Although the proposed work aims to solving a regression problem, it is just a straightforward replacement of the output layer comparing to classification.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
In this paper, authors claim that prognostic prediction modeled as a regression task rather than classification helps provide more granular estimates of disease progression. In the experimental design, a real measurement called CDRSB is used for evaluation. However, there are several concerns:
1)	Existing works on solving the progression prediction problems as a supervised classification task or an unsupervised structure learning problem are missing in the related works.
2)	How is the single measurement like CDRSB reliable enough to make accurate prediction or indicate the stage of the progression path? In the experiments, only R^2 is used as the evaluation criterion, is this metric correlated well to popularly used classification labels? How about the noisy CDRSB scores?

This paper mainly focuses on applying existing self-supervised deep CNN methods for regression problem in settings that previous works have already explored. From related work, self-supervised learning has already been used to solve various problems of the same domain. From modeling perspective, only output layer for classification needs to be replaced for regression. So, the technical novelty is weak.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed regression problem is not well justified in the application domain, and the technical contribution is weak.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper develops a cross-domain self-supervised learning approach for disease prognostic modeling as a regression problem using 3D images as input. Then, this paper also provides a detailed and extensive framework to evaluate the performance of the proposed model fine-tuned from different supervised and self-supervised models pre-trained on either natural images or medical images. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach to combat the lack of large-scale annotated data for training deep models for progression prediction.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

(1) The authors establish a cross-domain self-supervised transfer learning approach for medical image analysis that leverages self-supervised learning on both unlabeled large-scale natural images. 
(2) The authors provide a detailed and extensive framework to evaluate the performance of the proposed model fine-tuned from different supervised and self-supervised models pre-trained on either natural images or medical images.
(3) The overall structure is clear. 

Weakness:
(1) The authors only conduct a benchmarking analysis to evaluate the efficacy of different pre-training models for disease progression prediction as a regression problem, while there are not any new technologies in this paper. Thus, the overall novelty is very limited. 
(2) This paper mainly investigates cross-domain self-supervised deep learning for robust Alzheimer’s Disease progression modeling, thus it is recommended to evaluate these models by using classification metrics. 
(3) The authors should investigate the effects of different numbers of samples used in the pre-training and fine-tuning stages.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The overall structure is clear and well-written. However, the novelty is limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the paper is well-written and proposes a cross-domain self-supervised transfer learning approach for medical image analysis. My major concern is the novelty, as well as other evaluation metrics and comparison results.

content.title: Cross-Domain Self-Supervised Deep Learning for Robust Alzheimer's Disease Progression Modeling
content.abstract: Developing successful artificial intelligence systems in practice depends both on robust deep learning models as well as large high quality data. Acquiring and labeling data can become prohibitively expensive and time-consuming in many real-world applications such as clinical disease models. Self-supervised learning has demonstrated great potential in increasing model accuracy and robustness in small data regimes. In addition, many clinical imaging and disease modeling applications rely heavily on regression of continuous quantities. However, the applicability of self-supervised learning for these medical-imaging regression tasks has not been extensively studied. In this study, we develop a cross-domain self-supervised learning approach for disease prognostic modeling as a regression problem using 3D images as input. We demonstrate that self-supervised pre-training can improve the prediction of Alzheimer's Disease progression from brain MRI. We also show that pre-training on extended (but not labeled) brain MRI data outperforms pre-training on natural images. We further observe that the highest performance is achieved when both natural images and extended brain-MRI data are used for pre-training.
